title: 22. Interview: Leader Election
summary: Interview Q&A for Leader Election — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Leader Election interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Compare the Bully and Ring algorithms on message complexity, failure model, and partition tolerance.
**Answer:** The Bully algorithm has worst-case message complexity O(N²) — each node that starts an election messages all higher-id nodes, and the highest-id node then broadcasts to all. Best case (only the second-highest node starts) is O(N). The Ring algorithm also has O(N²) worst-case but O(N) best case. On failure model, both tolerate crash failures: as long as a majority of nodes are alive, an election completes. Neither tolerates network partitions: during a partition, each side can independently elect its own leader, causing split-brain — both algorithms assume a fully-connected network. The Ring algorithm has a slight operational advantage because each node only needs to know its successor (O(1) membership state), whereas Bully requires each node to know all higher-id nodes (O(N) state). Both are textbook algorithms, rarely used in pure form in production; they inform the design of voting-based algorithms (Raft, Paxos) which add quorum-based partition tolerance. The takeaway: Bully and Ring teach the principle of deterministic leader selection by id, but production systems always add quorums and fencing.
**Visual:**
```
Bully: each node -> all higher nodes  (O(N²) msgs), full membership (O(N) state)
Ring:  each node -> successor only     (O(N²) msgs, O(N) best), O(1) membership state
Both:  crash-tolerant (majority alive), NOT partition-tolerant (split-brain risk)
Production: add quorums (Raft/Paxos) + fencing tokens for partition safety
```

### Q2. Explain the Raft voting rules and how they prevent split-brain.
**Answer:** Raft's voting rules are: (1) each node has a current term (logical clock) and a voted-for record; (2) when a follower's election timer fires, it increments the term, becomes a candidate, votes for itself, and sends RequestVote RPCs to all other nodes; (3) a node grants its vote only if the candidate's term is ≥ its own AND it has not already voted in this term AND the candidate's log is at least as up-to-date as its own (compared by last log index and term); (4) a candidate wins if it receives votes from a strict majority of nodes; (5) if a node receives an RPC with a higher term, it immediately reverts to follower. These rules prevent split-brain through two mechanisms. First, the at-most-one-vote-per-term rule means at most one candidate can receive a majority in a given term (a majority is more than half, so two disjoint majorities would require more than N nodes). Second, the term-based rejection means a stale leader from an older term cannot commit writes: when it sends AppendEntries, followers reply with their higher term, causing the stale leader to step down. Together these guarantee that at most one valid leader exists at any time. The trade-off is that during a partition, the minority side cannot elect a leader (no majority) and is unavailable — the correct, safe behavior.
**Visual:**
```
term=3: A,B,C elect A (majority 2/3)
partition {A} | {B,C}:
  B,C increment to term=4, B wins majority (2/3)
  A (still term=3) sends AppendEntries -> B,C reject (term 4 > 3) -> A steps down
result: only B is valid leader (epoch=4); A's writes rejected by storage (fencing)
```

### Q3. What is a lease, and how does it improve leader election? What are its prerequisites?
**Answer:** A lease is a time-bounded grant of authority: the leader holds the right to act as leader for a fixed duration (e.g., 5 seconds) and must renew before expiry to retain leadership. If the leader crashes or partitions, the lease expires naturally and a new leader can be elected without waiting for a heartbeat-timeout-based failure detector — failover latency drops from the heartbeat timeout (typically 5-30 seconds) to the lease duration (often 1-5 seconds). Leases are used by Chubby (10-second default), ZooKeeper, etcd, and Kubernetes leader election. The prerequisites are: (1) bounded clock drift — all nodes must agree on the time within a known epsilon (NTP gives <10ms, GPS <1ms), because lease expiry is a wall-clock event; (2) the lease duration must exceed the worst-case clock drift plus the network round-trip, so a leader cannot believe it holds a lease after the cluster has expired it; (3) the leader must renew before expiry with enough margin to account for drift and network delay. The trade-off is that leases add operational complexity (clock management) and a small unavailability window during expiry if the renewal fails. The benefit is fast failover without false positives — the lease guarantees the old leader is dead before the new one is elected.
**Visual:**
```
leader holds lease for T=5s, renews at T=4s
  crash at T=2s -> no renewal -> lease expires at T=5s
  new leader election starts at T=5s (no heartbeat timeout wait)
prereqs:
  - bounded clock drift (NTP <10ms, GPS <1ms)
  - lease T >> drift + RTT
  - renew before expiry with safety margin
```

### Q4. What is a fencing token, and why is it necessary even with leader election?
**Answer:** A fencing token (also called epoch, term, generation number) is a monotonically increasing integer assigned to each leader. When a new leader is elected, the token increments, and every write the leader issues carries it. Storage systems track the highest token they have seen and reject writes with stale tokens. The necessity arises from a subtle race: even after a new leader is elected, the old leader may not yet know it has been deposed — it may be paused for GC, stuck in a partition, or simply slow. When the old leader resumes, it may issue a write to storage that has already accepted writes from the new leader. Without fencing, the storage would accept the stale write, corrupting the new leader's data. With fencing, the storage sees the stale token and rejects the write. This is the basis of HDFS's epoch-based NameNode failover, Kafka's leader epoch in the KRaft protocol, GFS's chunkserver lease revocation, and ZooKeeper's zxid. The fencing token turns leader election from "we agreed who the new leader is" into "we guarantee the old leader cannot make progress," closing the split-brain window.
**Visual:**
```
old leader L1 (token=5) pauses for GC during partition
new leader L2 (token=6) elected, writes "x=2" to storage (token=6)
L1 resumes, sends write "x=1" with token=5 to storage
storage: max_seen_token=6 > 5 -> REJECT (stale token)
result: L2's data is safe; L1's stale write is fenced off
```

### Q5. Why do even-sized clusters (4, 6) cause election problems, and how is this resolved?
**Answer:** In an even-sized cluster, a 50-50 partition splits the votes evenly, and neither side can reach a strict majority. With N=4 and a 2-2 split, no leader can be elected on either side, so the entire cluster becomes unavailable even though half the nodes are healthy on each side. This is strictly worse than an odd-sized cluster where one side always has the majority (e.g., N=3 with a 2-1 split, or N=5 with a 3-2 split). The standard resolutions are: (1) prefer odd cluster sizes (3, 5, 7) — this is the etcd/ZooKeeper/Consul recommendation; (2) use a witness node (a non-data-bearing tie-breaker) in a third location, so an even data-bearing cluster plus a witness gives an odd voting membership (the SQL Server AlwaysOn witness pattern); (3) accept the unavailability of even-sized clusters during evenly-split partitions and rely on operational monitoring to resolve the partition quickly. The witness approach is popular because it adds the tie-breaking vote without adding data-replication cost — the witness participates in elections but does not store user data, so it can run on a small, cheap instance. The architect's rule of thumb: if you must run an even number of data nodes (e.g., 4 for capacity reasons), add a witness to make the voting membership odd.
**Visual:**
```
N=4:  partition 2-2 -> neither side has majority -> full outage
N=3:  partition 2-1 -> majority side elects leader -> partial availability
N=5:  partition 3-2 -> majority side elects leader -> partial availability
N=4 + witness (voting only, no data): 4 data + 1 witness = 5 voters (odd) -> safe
```

### Q6. Compare leader election via etcd vs. via ZooKeeper vs. via a custom Bully implementation.
**Answer:** **etcd** (Raft-based) provides a lease + compare-and-set API: a candidate creates a lease, acquires a key with that lease (atomically), and becomes leader; if the leader's lease expires (process crash, network partition), the key is released and another candidate can acquire it. Kubernetes uses this for its scheduler and controller-manager leader election. **ZooKeeper** (Zab-based) provides ephemeral nodes: a candidate creates an ephemeral node; if the candidate's session expires (lost heartbeat), the node is deleted, and a watcher on the next candidate fires, triggering it to create its own node. Both etcd and ZooKeeper provide battle-tested, formally-proven election with built-in fencing (lease/epoch). A **custom Bully implementation** is the worst choice for production: it lacks partition tolerance (split-brain during network issues), lacks fencing (old leader's writes are not rejected), and the team must maintain the correctness proofs themselves. The trade-off between etcd and ZooKeeper is operational: etcd is Go-native and integrates well with Kubernetes; ZooKeeper is Java-based and is the standard in the Hadoop ecosystem (Kafka, HBase, Spark). For new systems, etcd is the default choice unless the surrounding ecosystem mandates ZooKeeper. The architect's rule: never implement leader election from scratch; use etcd or ZooKeeper.
**Visual:**
```
etcd:      lease + CAS on a key       (Go, Kubernetes-native)
ZK:        ephemeral node + watcher   (Java, Hadoop ecosystem)
custom Bully: NO partition tolerance, NO fencing, NO proofs -> AVOID
rule: use etcd or ZK; never roll your own for production correctness
```

### Q7. What is the "leaderless" architecture, and when is it preferable to leader election?
**Answer:** A leaderless architecture, exemplified by Amazon Dynamo and its open-source descendants (Cassandra, Riak, Voldemort), avoids electing a leader entirely. Every node can accept writes for any key (the key is hashed to a replica set, and the client contacts any replica in the set). Writes use quorum protocols (W of N) to commit; reads use quorum (R of N) to retrieve. There is no single point of failure and no leader-election unavailability window. The trade-offs: (1) writes require coordinating across multiple replicas per write (no leader to amortize the coordination); (2) conflict resolution must be handled per-key (LWW, vector clocks, CRDTs); (3) strong consistency is harder to achieve (requires R+W>N with version comparison, and even then conflicts can occur under concurrent writes). Leaderless is preferable for workloads with high write throughput, eventual-consistency tolerance, and no need for cross-key transactions — social feeds, recommendation counters, IoT telemetry, product catalogs. Leader-based (Raft, Paxos) is preferable for workloads requiring linearizability, low-latency reads from a single location, or cross-key transactions — configuration stores, lock services, financial ledgers. Many systems use a hybrid: leaderless for the data plane (high-throughput writes) and leader-based for the control plane (metadata, schema, configuration). The architect must understand that leader election is one design point, not a universal requirement.
**Visual:**
```
leader-based (Raft/Paxos): 1 leader accepts writes, replicates to followers
  + low read latency (read from leader), linearizable, cross-key txns
  - leader is bottleneck, election unavailability, write coord per entry
leaderless (Dynamo/Cassandra): any replica accepts writes, quorum commits
  + no single bottleneck, no election downtime, high write throughput
  - eventual consistency (typically), per-key conflict resolution
hybrid: leaderless data plane + leader-based control plane (common pattern)
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Your Kafka cluster uses ZooKeeper for controller election. The controller node crashes. Walk through the election process and the impact on producers and consumers.
**Answer:** When the Kafka controller (a special broker that manages partition leadership) crashes, ZooKeeper's ephemeral node for the controller disappears (the controller's ZK session expires after 6-18 seconds of lost heartbeats). Other brokers have a watch on this ephemeral node; the watch fires, and the brokers race to create a new controller node. The first broker to succeed (ZooKeeper guarantees only one creator) becomes the new controller. The new controller reads cluster state from ZooKeeper, identifies partitions whose leader was on the crashed broker, and elects new partition leaders from the in-sync replicas (ISRs) of those partitions. Producers and consumers see brief errors (NotLeaderForPartitionException) and must refresh metadata; modern Kafka clients do this automatically within ~1 second. The total recovery time is roughly: ZK session timeout (6-18s) + election (<1s) + partition leader election (1-2s) = 10-20 seconds of degraded throughput for affected partitions. With KRaft (Kafka's newer Raft-based metadata quorum, replacing ZooKeeper), the controller failover is faster (~1-2 seconds) because there is no ZK session-timeout wait. The lesson: the controller is a single point of coordination, and its failover window is the cluster's RTO for metadata operations.
**Visual:**
```
controller N1 crashes -> ZK session expires (6-18s)
  ephemeral node /controller deleted
  watchers on N2,N3 fire -> race to create /controller
  first to create wins -> new controller
  new controller re-elects partition leaders from ISRs
  clients: NotLeaderForPartitionException -> refresh metadata (~1s)
  total RTO: ~10-20s (ZK mode), ~1-2s (KRaft mode)
```

### Q2. You deploy Kubernetes with a 3-node etcd cluster. One etcd node's disk fills up, causing it to fall behind. The other two elect a new leader. What happens to the stalled node?
**Answer:** The stalled node cannot fsync its Raft log (disk full), so it cannot ack AppendEntries. The leader (one of the two healthy nodes) detects this via the lack of acks and marks the stalled node's `nextIndex` as behind. The healthy two nodes form a quorum and continue committing writes normally; Kubernetes API server continues to function via the healthy leader. The stalled node is effectively a "lagging follower" — it has not crashed, but it cannot catch up. When the disk is freed, the stalled node begins processing queued AppendEntries from the leader, which walks back its `nextIndex` until it finds a matching point, then streams the missing entries. This recovery is bandwidth-bound: a node that fell behind by 1GB of log will take ~10 seconds on a 1Gbps link to catch up. During the lag, the stalled node should not serve Kubernetes API requests (etcd's `--strict-reconfig-check` and the API server's readiness probe handle this). If the disk cannot be cleared quickly, the operator should remove the stalled node from the cluster (`etcdctl member remove`), free the disk, re-add it as a fresh member, and let it stream a full snapshot. The takeaway: disk-full conditions are a common production failure mode for etcd, and the recovery is automatic once the underlying issue is resolved.
**Visual:**
```
3-node etcd: {A, B, C}, C's disk fills
  C cannot fsync -> cannot ack AppendEntries
  A, B form quorum, continue committing writes (cluster OK)
  C is "lagging follower" (alive but behind)
disk freed -> C processes queued AppendEntries
  leader walks back nextIndex, streams missing entries
  recovery time = log_lag / bandwidth (1GB / 1Gbps = 10s)
if disk not clearable: remove C, free disk, re-add as fresh member (full snapshot)
```

### Q3. Your team is building a scheduled-job system where one of 10 worker nodes must run a cron job every minute. They propose using a database row with a "current_runner" column and a `SELECT FOR UPDATE` to elect the runner. What are the issues?
**Answer:** Three issues with this design. First, the `SELECT FOR UPDATE` approach does not handle the runner crashing mid-job: if the runner crashes after acquiring the lock but before completing the job, the lock is held until the connection times out (typically 30-60 seconds), during which no other worker can run the job — the cron schedule is missed. Second, the database becomes a single point of failure and a bottleneck: every worker contends for the same row, causing lock contention and reduced throughput as the worker count grows. Third, there is no fencing: if the runner's network connection to the database drops after it has started the job, the database will eventually release the lock and another worker will start the same job — but the original runner may still be running, leading to duplicate execution. The correct design is to use a lease-based election: each worker acquires a lease (in etcd, ZooKeeper, or even the database with a lease column that includes an expiry timestamp). The runner renews the lease periodically while running; if it crashes, the lease expires and another worker takes over. For exactly-once execution of side-effecting jobs, the job itself must be idempotent (so duplicates are safe) or use a fencing token to gate the side effect (e.g., a unique job-idempotency-key checked at the destination).
**Visual:**
```
SELECT FOR UPDATE: lock held until conn close or timeout
  - runner crash mid-job: lock held 30-60s -> schedule missed
  - db single point of failure + bottleneck
  - no fencing: network drop -> duplicate execution
fix: lease-based election (etcd/ZK lease with expiry + renew)
  - job idempotent OR fencing token at side-effect destination
```

### Q4. A 5-node Raft cluster is partitioned 3-2. The 3-node side continues as the majority. A client on the 2-node side needs to write. What happens?
**Answer:** The 2-node side is the minority and cannot elect a leader (Raft requires 3 of 5 votes). The client's writes to the 2-node side will fail with a "no leader" or "not quorum" error, because neither of the 2 nodes can commit a write without a third ack. This is the correct, safe behavior — without it, the minority side would accept writes that conflict with the majority side's writes, causing split-brain. The client has two options. First, the client should retry against the majority side: production Raft clients (e.g., etcd's go client) maintain a list of all endpoints and automatically retry against the leader; if the client is configured to know all 5 nodes, it will find the leader on the 3-node side. Second, if the client cannot reach the majority side (e.g., it is itself partitioned on the 2-node side), it must fail the write and inform the user — there is no way to make a strongly-consistent write during a partition that puts the client on the minority side. For workloads that must remain available during such partitions (e.g., a regional e-commerce site), the architecture should be designed so that each region owns its own data and uses a separate quorum per region, with async cross-region replication — this avoids any cross-region quorum dependency. The takeaway: Raft's unavailability on the minority side is the price of safety.
**Visual:**
```
5-node Raft, partition 3-2:
  3-node side: elects leader, commits writes (majority)
  2-node side: no leader (need 3 votes, have 2) -> writes FAIL
client on 2-node side:
  retry against 3-node side (etcd client auto-discovers leader)
  if client itself partitioned: write fails (must inform user)
lesson: strong consistency requires majority side reachability
```

### Q5. You run a 3-node MongoDB replica set. The primary crashes during a large index build. The two secondaries elect a new primary, but the new primary does not have the index. What happens?
**Answer:** MongoDB's index builds are not replicated as in-progress state; instead, the build is initiated on the primary, and the index-build operation is replicated to the secondaries via the oplog. If the primary crashes mid-build, the oplog entries for the index build have been replicated to the secondaries up to the point of crash. The new primary (one of the secondaries) will continue the index build from where its oplog left off — if the index-build oplog entries have been applied, the index is partially built and MongoDB will roll back the partial build and restart from the beginning (or, depending on version, resume from a checkpoint). The exact behavior depends on the MongoDB version: pre-4.2 builds were foreground-blocking and would restart from scratch on failover; 4.2+ builds use a two-phase build with checkpoints that can resume. The index is unavailable for queries until the build completes. The application impact: queries that relied on the index will fall back to a collection scan (slow) or fail if the query requires the index. The operator's response: monitor the index build progress (`db.currentOp()`), wait for it to complete, and ensure the application can degrade gracefully during the window. The lesson: long-running operations like index builds and migrations should be designed to be resumable and idempotent, because leader changes during the operation are inevitable in production.
**Visual:**
```
primary N1 starts index build (large collection)
  oplog entries replicated to N2, N3 (build progresses on secondaries in parallel)
N1 crashes mid-build
  N2 or N3 elected new primary
  new primary resumes build from checkpoint (4.2+) OR restarts (pre-4.2)
  index unavailable -> queries degrade (collection scan) or fail
operator: monitor db.currentOp(), wait for completion, plan for degraded queries
```

### Q6. Your system uses Redis Sentinel for leader election of a "primary cache." During a network blip, two Sentinels promote different nodes. How do you detect, prevent, and recover?
**Answer:** This is the classic Sentinel split-brain scenario. Detection: monitor for two nodes both believing they are primary (Redis's `INFO replication` command on each node shows `role:master` for both); monitor client errors for conflicting writes (the same key has different values on the two nodes); enable Redis's `min-replicas-to-write` config, which prevents a primary from accepting writes if it cannot see enough replicas — if both nodes have this config, only one will be writable, reducing (but not eliminating) split-brain. Prevention: (1) use Redis 6+ with the Raft-based leader election in Redis Cluster (not Sentinel); (2) add a witness node in a third location for tie-breaking; (3) use `min-replicas-to-write 1` and `min-replicas-max-lag 10` so a partitioned primary that loses its replicas stops accepting writes; (4) accept that Sentinel is not formally proven and switch to etcd-based election for systems where correctness matters. Recovery: (1) identify which node has the most recent consistent data (typically the one with the highest offset); (2) demote the other node with `REPLICAOF <winner-ip> <port>`; (3) let the demoted node resync from the winner (it will discard its divergent writes); (4) audit application logs for any writes that the demoted node accepted and the winner did not — these are lost and may need manual reconciliation. The lesson: Sentinel is fine for caching scenarios where occasional data loss is tolerable; for invariant-bearing state, use a proven consensus system.
**Visual:**
```
detection:  both nodes report role:master -> split-brain
            conflicting values for same key on two nodes
prevention: Redis Cluster Raft (6+) OR min-replicas-to-write=1
            OR witness node OR switch to etcd
recovery:   pick winner (highest replication offset)
            demote loser (REPLICAOF winner)
            audit app logs for lost writes (manual reconciliation)
```

### Q7. You are designing a multi-region service where each region has a leader for its local data, but a global coordinator must orchestrate cross-region operations. How do you architect the leader election?
**Answer:** Use a two-tier architecture. Tier 1 (regional): each region runs its own Raft group (3 nodes per region) for its local data; regional leaders are elected within their region with sub-second failover. This gives each region low-latency local writes and survives regional node failures. Tier 2 (global): a separate small Raft group (3 nodes, one per region) acts as the global coordinator; it tracks which region is the "owner" of each cross-region resource and orchestrates cross-region operations. The global coordinator is elected via the same Raft protocol, with cross-region round trips giving ~50-150ms commit latency — acceptable for the low volume of global coordination. Cross-region operations use 2PC: the global coordinator (Tier 2 leader) initiates a 2PC across the regional leaders (Tier 1), each of which commits its part via its regional Raft group. If the global coordinator fails, the Tier 2 Raft group elects a new one in ~1-2 seconds. The architecture is essentially Spanner's: per-shard Paxos groups for data, a global Paxos group for the transaction coordinator, with 2PC across groups for distributed transactions. The trade-off is complexity — two tiers of consensus, 2PC for cross-region ops — but it gives regional autonomy for the common case and global linearizability for the rare cross-region case.
**Visual:**
```
Tier 1 (regional):  us-east Raft {A,B,C}, eu-west Raft {D,E,F}, asia Raft {G,H,I}
                    regional leader per region, sub-second failover, local writes
Tier 2 (global):    global Raft {one node per region: A, D, G}
                    coordinator for cross-region resources, ~50-150ms commit
cross-region txn:   2PC initiated by Tier 2 leader, Tier 1 leaders participate
                    each Tier 1 leader commits via regional Raft
failover:           Tier 1 -> regional (~1s); Tier 2 -> global (~1-2s cross-region)
```
